content: Children with severe acute malnutrition (SAM) and non-severe tuberculosis (TB) should ideally receive a six-month TB treatment regimen. This recommendation is based on the limited evidence available for this subgroup and the recognition of SAM as a danger sign. Infants younger than three months of age or weighing less than 3 kg, including those born prematurely (less than 37 weeks gestation), were excluded from the SHINE trial. There is no new data available on the treatment of congenital TB or TB in very young infants (aged 0–3 months). For infants in this age group with suspected or confirmed pulmonary TB (PTB) or tuberculous peripheral lymphadenitis, treatment should follow the six-month regimen (2HRZ(E)/4HR) as outlined in the 2014 WHO guidance for national TB programs. Dose adjustments may be necessary to account for age-related factors and potential toxicity, and such decisions should be made by clinicians experienced in managing pediatric TB. Children and adolescents who have been treated for TB in the past two years are at increased risk of treatment failure and drug resistance. These individuals were excluded from the SHINE trial and should be treated with the standard six-month regimen (2HRZ(E)/4HR). Assessing the severity of TB disease is a critical implementation consideration, particularly in settings without access to chest radiography (CXR) or WHO-recommended diagnostic tests. CXR is considered a vital tool for evaluating the severity of intrathoracic disease. Non-severe intrathoracic or PTB disease is defined as intrathoracic lymph node TB without airway obstruction, uncomplicated TB pleural effusion, or paucibacillary, non-cavitary disease confined to one lung lobe without a miliary pattern. Extensive or advanced disease in children under 15 years is typically characterized by the presence of cavities or bilateral disease on CXR. National TB programs (NTPs) are encouraged to expand access to quality CXR and train healthcare providers in its interpretation. However, out-of-pocket expenses for CXR may pose a barrier to TB diagnosis and access to shorter regimens for eligible children and adolescents. In the SHINE trial, children who were Xpert MTB/RIF positive but sputum smear-negative were eligible for inclusion. Among the 85 children (7%) who were Xpert MTB/RIF positive, most had very low or low semi-quantitative results. Detailed implementation guidance is provided in the operational handbook on managing TB in children and adolescents, considering differences in healthcare systems and country contexts, including the availability of diagnostic tools to assess disease severity. While access to CXR is important, it should not prevent children and adolescents in resource-limited settings from benefiting from shorter regimens. Children with Xpert MTB/RIF or Ultra results that are trace, very low, or low, and who meet radiographic or clinical criteria for non-severe TB, can be treated with the four-month regimen. The continuum between TB infection and disease is another important consideration. Shorter treatment regimens for drug-susceptible TB are now similar in duration and composition to recently recommended shorter regimens for treating TB infection, such as the three-month daily isoniazid and rifampicin regimen (3HR). Misdiagnosing a child with TB infection as having non-severe TB disease may not have severe consequences. Scaling up contact investigation approaches can improve early identification of children with non-severe disease who may benefit from the four-month regimen. In settings with low HIV prevalence or low isoniazid resistance, children and young adolescents with non-severe TB who are HIV-negative can be treated with a three-drug regimen (HRZ) for two months, followed by two months of HR. In high HIV prevalence or high isoniazid resistance settings, children should be treated with HRZE for two months, followed by HR for two months. Ethambutol was used in the SHINE trial in line with these recommendations. NTPs are encouraged to prioritize child-friendly fixed-dose combination (FDC) formulations for TB treatment in children up to 25 kg body weight, such as the 3-FDC HRZ 50/75/150 mg with or without dispersible ethambutol, and the 2-FDC HR 50/75 mg. Capacity building for healthcare workers at all levels of the health system on diagnostic approaches, treatment decision algorithms, eligibility for the four-month regimen, and monitoring of children on first-line TB treatment is critical for successful implementation. Children and young adolescents with forms of PTB that do not meet eligibility criteria for the four-month regimen should be treated with the standard six-month regimen, which includes a fourth drug (ethambutol) in the intensive phase (e.g., 2HRZE/4HR). Adolescents aged 12 years and above with TB can benefit from the four-month regimen consisting of isoniazid, rifapentine, moxifloxacin, and pyrazinamide (HPMZ), which is conditionally recommended by WHO. Adolescents aged 12–16 years have three treatment options: the four-month HPMZ regimen, the four-month 2HRZ(E)/2HR regimen, and the standard six-month 2HRZ(E)/4HR regimen. Adolescents aged 16 years and above, who were not included in the SHINE trial, have two options: the four-month HPMZ regimen and the standard six-month 2HRZE/4HR regimen. The choice of regimen for this age group depends on clinical factors (e.g., presence of severe disease, HIV status, and CD4 count) and contextual factors (e.g., availability of the HPMZ regimen in the country). Clinical monitoring requirements for the shorter regimen are the same as for the six-month regimen, and treatment outcomes are determined at the end of the four-month regimen. If there is insufficient clinical improvement after completing the four-month regimen, the clinician may extend treatment to six months while considering alternative diagnoses, including drug-resistant TB. Monitoring for potential relapse is a priority for shorter regimens, especially when introduced in programmatic settings. Follow-up of children and young adolescents for up to 12 months after completing the four-month regimen is important. WHO currently recommends a 12-month regimen for treating TB meningitis (TBM), consisting of isoniazid, rifampicin, ethambutol, and pyrazinamide daily for the first two months, followed by isoniazid and rifampicin daily for 10 additional months (2HRZE/10HR). This recommendation is based on a literature review and was first included in the 2010 rapid advice on TB treatment in children. Shorter regimens for pediatric TBM are used in some settings, such as South Africa, where a six-month regimen (6HRZEto) is recommended. However, these recommendations are based on expert opinion, and a clinical trial is underway to compare a six-month regimen with the WHO-recommended 12-month regimen. Results are expected in 2023. Shorter regimens may improve adherence and reduce the burden on patients and healthcare systems, but it is not yet known how outcomes compare to the 12-month regimen.
